common_name: Red Champ Mayhaw (Large-Fruited Dark Red Western Mayhaw)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil in full sun; Red Champ blooms somewhat later than older mayhaw selections, which can help the crop escape a late freeze, and benefits from a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Red Champ is a named western mayhaw selection grown for its large, dark red fruit and heavy, reliable yields, making it a popular choice among commercial mayhaw growers in Louisiana and East Texas. It shows good resistance to fire blight compared with many older mayhaw selections, an important trait in the humid Gulf Coast climate where the disease is a persistent risk to hawthorns and other rosaceous fruit trees. Like other mayhaws it thrives in moist to wet, acidic, poorly drained soil where many other fruit trees struggle, reflecting its origin as a native wetland species. Plant alongside another mayhaw cultivar for cross-pollination, and expect the tart, aromatic fruit each spring to be prized mainly for jelly, syrup, and wine rather than fresh eating.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter -- Mayhaw Production and Culture
Just Fruits and Exotics nursery catalog
Mississippi State University Extension -- Mayhaw Diseases

common_name: Sherwood Akins Mayhaw (Large-Fruited Late-Season Western Mayhaw)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil in full sun; this later-blooming, later-ripening selection benefits from a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Sherwood Akins is a named western mayhaw selection grown for producing some of the largest fruit found among mayhaw cultivars, blooming and ripening later in the season than most other named selections. As with other mayhaws, it is a wetland-adapted small tree that performs best in moist to wet, acidic soil and benefits from a second mayhaw cultivar planted nearby to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set. The glossy red fruit ripens in late spring into the tart, highly aromatic berries traditionally gathered along Gulf South bayous and sloughs for homemade jelly and syrup. Site away from eastern redcedar where practical, since mayhaws can be affected by cedar-apple and cedar-hawthorn rust in areas where the alternate host is common.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter -- Mayhaw Production and Culture

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and needs no separate pollinator, and Krasnoslobodskaya is a cold-hardy Russian selection traditionally grown in the Lower Volga region.

directions: Krasnoslobodskaya is a quince cultivar long grown in the Lower Volga region of Russia, where it is valued for tolerating a colder, more continental climate than many of the Mediterranean and Balkan quince selections more commonly sold in the United States. Like other quince, it is self-fertile and produces hard, intensely aromatic golden fruit in fall that is cooked into jelly, paste, or preserves rather than eaten raw. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune to an open form to maintain good air circulation, which helps reduce fire blight risk during the humid Gulf Coast growing season. Harvest once fruit turns fully golden and develops its characteristic strong perfume, then store in a cool, dry location where quince keeps notably longer than most other tree fruit.
sources: Agricultural Research Information System (AGRIS) -- quince nursery development literature
Siberian Journal of Life Sciences and Agriculture

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and needs no separate pollinator, and Morava is a vigorous Serbian selection evaluated alongside other Balkan quince cultivars in regional growth trials.

directions: Morava is a Serbian quince cultivar that showed among the strongest vigor of the selections evaluated in a multi-year growth and yield trial conducted in the Belgrade region, growing somewhat larger and more vigorously than many other named Balkan quince cultivars. Like other quince, it is self-fertile and bears hard, highly fragrant golden-yellow fruit in fall that is traditionally cooked into jelly, paste, or preserves. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and allow extra spacing given its above-average vigor; prune to an open vase form to keep good air circulation through the canopy, which is the main defense against fire blight in humid climates. Harvest once the fruit turns fully golden and gives off its characteristic strong aroma.
sources: International Society for Horticultural Science (ISHS) -- quince cultivar growth and yield trial, Belgrade region

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile, though Hemus sets slightly better with a second cultivar such as Portugal or Asenica nearby, and it ripens early, in the first third of October.

directions: Hemus is a Bulgarian quince cultivar bred at a fruit research institute in Plovdiv, selected for an unusually broad tolerance of different soils and climates compared with older European quince selections. It bears large, pear-to-apple-shaped fruit that ripens to a light lemon-yellow in early fall, with a sweet-sour flavor noted as especially good for processing into jelly, paste, and preserves. The tree is self-fertile but fruits a bit more heavily with a second quince cultivar planted nearby. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune for an open canopy to encourage air movement, which helps limit fire blight in humid regions like the Gulf Coast.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile, though Asenica sets slightly better with a second cultivar such as Hemus or Portugal nearby, and it ripens in mid-October.

directions: Asenica is a Bulgarian quince cultivar producing large, conical, lemon-yellow fruit covered in a light fuzz, weighing from roughly a half pound up to over a pound each at harvest in mid-October. The flesh is mildly acidic, tender, and aromatic by quince standards, and the cultivar is noted as suitable for fresh use in addition to the cooked preserves, pastes, and jellies that most quince are traditionally used for. The tree is self-fertile but benefits from a second quince cultivar nearby for improved fruit set. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, prune to an open form for good air circulation, and watch for fire blight, the main disease risk for quince in humid climates such as the Gulf Coast.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile, though Triumph sets slightly better with a second cultivar such as Portugal nearby, and it ripens from mid to late October.

directions: Triumph is a vigorous quince cultivar that forms a rounded crown and fruits reliably year after year, bearing greenish-yellow, slightly fuzzy, pear-shaped fruit that averages close to a pound each. The flesh is notably sour even by quince standards, balanced by a strong, pleasant aroma, making it well suited to jelly, paste, and syrup once cooked with sugar. The tree is self-fertile but fruits more heavily with a second quince cultivar planted nearby. Grow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune to an open vase shape to maintain good air circulation, which is the main defense against fire blight in humid climates like the Gulf Coast.
